transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-22 09:23 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Devon (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Product), Michael (Atlas ML), Aisha (Atlas SRE), Tom (Atlas Security), Nina (Atlas PM)

Summary: Quick console walkthrough focused on tracing, error analysis, and request logs for debugging production inference issues. Customer wants to understand how Redwood surfaces failing requests, latency hotspots, and how to run targeted repros / benchmarks. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private considerations for debug data and KMS/HSM integration. Agreed next step: run a 1-week pilot benchmark with request log capture and alerting configured.

Topics: console tracing overview; request logs and sample payload; error analysis flow; correlation of traces to request IDs and model versions; secure log access and retention; debug runbooks and automated alerting; pilot scope and timeline

Transcript body:
00:00 Sofia: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Devon my SE is with me and Priya from product will hop in for the console bits. How's Atlas doing this morning?
00:08 Michael: Good morning, doing well, thanks. We wanted to focus mostly on observability and debugging, specifically how you trace requests end-to-end and surface errors for our inference endpoints.
00:18 Devon: Great, that's exactly what we planned to show — the tracing tab in Redwood Console, request logs, and how error analysis ties back to model versions and routes. We'll try to keep it focused and demo a quick failing request scenario.
00:29 Nina: Quick note — we have regulatory constraints, so please cover private deployment and KMS options briefly.
00:34 Tom: And retention for logs, that's critical for audits.
00:37 Devon: Absolutely, we'll cover retention and role-based access as part of the security talk.
00:42 Sofia: Quick agenda — 1) tracing overview 2) error analysis walkthrough 3) request logs and sample payloads 4) pilot ask and next steps. Cool?
00:49 Aisha: Sounds good.

02:05 Devon: Okay jumping in — this is the Redwood Console, top nav -> Observability -> Tracing. Each trace is a single inference request lifecycle, we instrument kernel selection, routing, batching, KV cache hits, and model exec spans. You can filter by route, model, or request id.
02:24 Devon: Note, transcription may have noise here — some labels are auto-generated; model names can be truncated, e.g., "rwd-4b-quant" might show up as "rw4b-q" in the UI in narrow view.

04:10 Devon: Here's a sample trace where latency spikes at the "compile/kernel select" span — you can expand spans to see GPU utilization and selected kernel version, also config used (quantization profile, batch size).
04:28 Michael: Can you filter to just our customer namespace? We want to make sure we only see Atlas traffic during the pilot.
04:33 Devon: Yes filter by tenant — top-left tenant selector. For hosted pilot we can give you a dedicated tenant with isolation; for Dedicated/Private we map to your VPC or private cluster.
04:45 Michael: For private, can we control where traces are stored? We prefer logs to remain inside our VPC.
04:50 Priya: For Private deployments we offer local storage options and you can configure KMS for encryption-at-rest — logs can be routed to your S3 compatible bucket in your VPC or to an on-prem archive.

08:05 Devon: Switching to Error Analysis view — this aggregates failed requests by error class (model OOM, timeout, invalid input, quota). You can drill into a failure group and see sample requests, stack traces, and the trace id.
08:22 Devon: Example — this group shows a recurring "kv cache mismatch" error when sequence length exceeds 2048 on an older model variant, we recommend quantized model v2.1 or bumping the sequence config.
08:38 Aisha: Do you persist request payloads or just metadata? For HIPAA we can't store PHI payloads outside.
08:44 Devon: We store request metadata and can redact or omit payloads. For Private/Dedicated pilots we can configure zero-payload retention or local-only payload retention controlled by your policy.
08:56 Tom: How long do you retain traces by default? We have 13 months for audit.
09:01 Priya: Default hosted retention is 90 days for traces and 30 days for request payloads, but for enterprise we offer extended retention add-ons and on Private you control retention policy. We'll surface cost implications in the contract.

12:15 Devon: Now the request logs tab — it's a time-series and raw view. You can search by request id, route, user id, model version, or latency percentile. When you click an entry it opens the trace in context.
12:35 Devon: I'll simulate a failing request — sending a malformed chat message that triggers a "structure parse error".
12:42 (sound of keyboard)
12:48 Devon: Here we see the request log entry: timestamp, route, client_ip (obfuscated in hosted), model_version, token_count, latency_ms, error_type.
13:03 Michael: Can we export logs to our Splunk/Datadog?
13:08 Devon: Yes, we have integrations — streaming export to SIEMs via Kinesis/Firehose or direct API push. For Private you can push to your internal logging pipeline.

16:22 Devon: Correlating traces to request logs is key — each request has a unique request id and a trace id. You can search the request id in the Console search and it will show both the raw payload (if retained) and the trace timeline.
16:38 Michael: Ok so if we run a benchmark and see a 99th percentile latency spike, we can jump from the metric to concrete failing requests and the exact span causing the delay?
16:45 Devon: Exactly — the metrics link to sample traces with pre-filtered traces by the same anomaly pattern.

19:10 Aisha: How does batching affect trace visibility? If multiple logical user requests are batched into a single GPU invocation, can we still see logical request boundaries?
19:20 Devon: Yes, we expose logical borders — the trace has micro-spans for queueing and batching, and each logical request gets its own child span and request id. That way you can see which logical request in the batch incurred the model slowdown.

22:05 Devon: Demoing a debugging flow — find failing request -> open trace -> inspect spans -> identify hotspot (e.g., kv-cache miss) -> look at model version and kernel selection -> reproduce locally with same model variant and quant profile.
22:28 Michael: For reproduction, can we pull a sample payload and run it on our side?
22:33 Devon: If payload retention is enabled, yes — we'll give you access; otherwise we can provide sanitized sample or replay helper that strips PII.

26:10 Priya: On alerting — you can configure automatic alerts on error rates, latency percentiles, or custom log patterns. Alerts support webhook, PagerDuty, and email. You can tie alerts to runbooks that contain quick links to the trace and common remediation steps.
26:32 Nina: Are runbooks editable by us? We want our SREs to own the remediation steps.
26:36 Priya: Yes, runbooks are editable and you can scope them per-team with RBAC so only your SREs can modify.

30:00 Devon: Security specifics — SSO / SAML for console access, SCIM for provisioning, RBAC with granular scopes, and KMS support for model artifacts and logs. On Private we can integrate with customer HSM/KMS.
30:18 Tom: If we use customer-managed KMS, do logs get encrypted with our keys?
30:22 Priya: Yes, everything stored in your private deployment can be encrypted with your KMS keys; hosted options support envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key for enterprise plans.

33:55 Devon: Now a quick walkthrough of a recent incident analysis — show a group of errors that correlated with a kernel regression after a model patch. We use the tracing timelines to roll back traffic to a previous model variant via rollout policies.
34:13 Michael: How easy is a rollback? Can it be automated on error spike?
34:19 Devon: You can configure automatic fallback policies — e.g., if error rate > X or latency > Y for N minutes, traffic snaps back to the last-good model. That is part of the rollout toolset.

37:00 Aisha: For the pilot benchmark, how do we instrument synthetic traffic without corrupting metrics? We want to keep production metrics separate.
37:08 Devon: We typically provision a dedicated tenant or a separate route flagged as "benchmark". We also add traffic tags so metrics and traces are isolated. We'll show you a small script to generate realistic load and payload diversity.

41:22 Devon: Quick look at the request logs export — you can set a retention policy per route and per-content-type, e.g., redact payloads for certain routes. Exports support gzip and parquet for efficient storage.
41:41 Tom: For audits we may need raw logs for 13 months, is that possible?
41:46 Priya: Yes, with the extended retention add-on or Private deployment you can meet that requirement. We'll include cost projection in the contract.

45:30 Michael: Performance question — if we enable request logging with full payloads, what's the overhead on latency and cost?
45:38 Devon: Minimal on latency because logging is async; cost is mainly storage and export bandwidth. We do provide sampling and selective logging so you can capture 100% of errors but sample 1% of successes.

48:10 Sofia: Recap — Pilot: 1-week benchmark on a dedicated tenant, Atlas to provide sample traffic and baseline metrics, Redwood to provide pricing for extended retention and KMS options, security docs to be shared by Devon. Action items: Sofia send pricing, Devon send security + network diagram, Michael to share traffic.
48:34 Michael: Sounds good. We'll aim to have sample data by Friday.
48:39 Sofia: Great, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for kickoff and a tech onboarding session.

51:00 Tom: One last question — can we do a short POC on Private deployment later? We want to validate HSM integration before committing.
51:08 Sofia: Yes, that's a normal path — we can scope a Private POC after the hosted pilot if needed.

52:00 Devon: Thanks everyone, we'll send the follow-ups.

(End of recording)
